rationale: The 40-page version posted October 31, 2024 compares SOD1 in postmortem Parkinson brain tissue and examines a mouse model. The mouse report measures latency to fall in a motor task. Orange marks figure elements and copper-related annotations. The study does not compare citrus intake or measure how often people with Parkinson disease fall.

The 43-page version posted August 21, 2025 reports recordings in 35 people with Parkinson disease and targeted adaptive stimulation comparisons in subsets. It assesses mobility and freezing during walking and turning. Orange dots label turns in an extended-data figure. Discussion of fall risk supplies context without measuring an effect of raw orange.

The authenticated original abstract and Crossref verify the two-dye microarray methods paper on pages 1–8. The publisher endpoint returned a record without the body. The linked PMC7134330 is a conference collection with a different DOI. Obtain the exact published methods article and keep the conference collection separate.

The full original compares pedunculopontine and subthalamic neural recordings during imagined gait and control tasks in Parkinson disease. Orange denotes plotted neural locations or conditions. The experiment measures neural activity during gait imagery and records no dietary intake or actual fall frequency.

The complete issue member on pages 1410–1414 records prior falls and autopsy findings in a patient with the disorder the original calls Hallervorden-Spatz disease. Orange G is a staining name. Dietary deficiency is discussed as a possible comparison for organ findings. No intact orange exposure or Parkinson fall-frequency comparison is documented.

The full original uses single-cell RNA sequencing to compare developing ventral midbrain cells across species and stem-cell-derived preparations. Figure panels use orange for dividing cells or clusters. The study measures developmental cell states without a dietary or clinical falls comparison.

The study measures aggregation of alpha-synuclein constructs in solution. Orange and other colors distinguish construct signals in assay plots. There is no ingested citrus exposure or clinical fall measurement.

The full case reports multiday sleep and wake variation in dementia with Lewy bodies, including prolonged polysomnography. Orange is the trace color for eye movements. The case supplies sleep physiology rather than a citrus exposure or fall-frequency comparison.

The accepted original manuscript examines serious hypoglycaemia events in higher-risk older veterans over time and compares medication and disease characteristics. Any dietary treatment discussion concerns diabetes care. The outcome is hypoglycaemia-related acute care, without a raw-orange Parkinson fall estimate.

The retrospective original compares two irrigation approaches for chronic subdural haematoma and reports postoperative imaging and clinical outcomes. Orange arrows label scan findings. The comparison is surgical and provides no evidence on raw orange and Parkinson falls.

The article assesses welfare indicators and categorical thresholds on beef cattle farms. Orange denotes an intermediate category in the scoring. There is no human Parkinson cohort, citrus intervention or clinical fall outcome.

The original records stimulation-related brain activity and identifies two differing response circuits in 14 Parkinson patients undergoing subthalamic deep brain stimulation. Orange labels imaging or experimental conditions. Fall asleep is an instruction context and does not describe a fall event. The report gives no orange intake or fall-frequency comparison.

The clinical original describes cerebral amyloid angiopathy and cognitive decline associated with PSEN1 variants, including a fall recorded with gait ataxia. Orange is a figure annotation. The case does not compare intact citrus consumption or the frequency of falls in diagnosed Parkinson disease.

The protocol describes remote emergency neurological consultation versus usual care in non-stroke conditions. Orange boxes label possible paths in the design diagram. It includes no observed comparison of raw orange intake and Parkinson falls.

The retrospective Parkinson cohort compares balance response to levodopa with postsurgical balance after subthalamic stimulation. The primary balance measure is the Berg Balance Scale, with separate follow-up and medication conditions. Orange marks plotted values. Balance scores are not a count of falls, and there is no citrus exposure.

The autopsy-confirmed progressive apraxia of speech cohort links clinical speech progression to pathology, genetics, and neuroimaging. Orange marks imaging significance or contrast. The original does not study dietary citrus or attributable fall frequency in Parkinson disease.

The chemistry original compares multivalent ligand binding to several amyloid aggregates. Orange identifies tau in one plotted comparison. Its experimental outcomes are binding measurements, with no dietary exposure or clinical fall recording.

The original reports two people with SYNJ1-related early-onset parkinsonism treated with deep brain stimulation and compares them with a local genetic parkinsonism series. The evidence describes individual motor, medication, and gait outcomes. It contributes no controlled citrus intake or raw-orange effect on falls.

The original single-case report compares narrowband cortical gamma during stimulation of distinct basal ganglia targets. Orange marks electrode locations in a figure. The measured electrophysiological endpoint does not test raw-orange intake or clinical falls.

The case describes a mechanical fall and subsequent investigation of cirrhosis-associated parkinsonism that mimicked Parkinson disease. Orange arrows identify changes on imaging. The isolated fall, distinct diagnosis and absence of a measured citrus exposure do not supply the frozen claim comparison.

The short-term comparison investigates heart-rate variability after atomoxetine or placebo in Parkinson disease. Orange labels estimates for a study condition. Cardiac variability is the measured endpoint and the report supplies no raw-orange intake or fall-frequency result.

All four printed pages 186–189 describe acute levodopa response with entacapone or placebo. The authors note transient orange urine and a fall in plasma levodopa concentrations. These words refer to drug exposure and pharmacokinetics. The study does not measure citrus intake or how often patients fall.

All 15 printed pages 2368–2382 describe a laboratory study of bacterial movement responses. Orange describes an optical filter and fall refers to a decrease in a measured quantity. The source supplies no human Parkinson or culinary comparison.

The journal and publisher records corroborate the optic neuropathy letter at pages 196–202. The PMC views give a PDF pointer without original text. The publisher route and Europe PMC request supplied no readable original and the Cloud Service listed no public asset. Obtain the exact journal member to verify its exposure and clinical scope.

The journal records corroborate the CFTR letter at pages 195–196, with a distinct DOI and PMCID. The two PMC views and publisher paths supply no readable case or methods. The PMC Cloud Service listed no public asset. Obtain the exact letter to confirm its clinical boundaries.

The indexed printed article text matches the journal title and pages 189–192. The report concerns an SRY variant, ovarian function and the related clinical genetic investigation. The original case scope is identifiable without relying on the PMC PDF response, which did not yield a readable file. It supplies no dietary or Parkinson fall comparison.
